concepts.name: Tectonic Causes of Earthquakes: Fault Types and Stress Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Types of faults (normal, reverse, strike-slip, oblique) and associated plate boundary settings
Elastic rebound theory — mechanism of stress accumulation and sudden release
Distinction between interplate vs. intraplate earthquakes and why intraplate quakes (e.g., Koyna, Bhuj) are anomalous
UPSC trap: Convergent boundaries produce both reverse/thrust faults AND subduction-zone megathrusts — students confuse the two

concepts.name: Non-Tectonic Causes of Earthquakes: Volcanic, Collapse, and Reservoir-Induced Seismicity
key_dimensions: Volcanic earthquakes — magma movement as trigger; association with hotspots and rift zones
Reservoir-Induced Seismicity (RIS) — mechanism of pore-pressure increase and lubrication of faults (Koyna Dam case study)
Collapse earthquakes in karst/mining regions — distinguishing from tectonic events
UPSC trap: RIS is an anthropogenic cause — frequently tested in context of large dams and environmental impact

concepts.name: Focus (Hypocenter) vs. Epicenter: Geometry and Depth Classification
key_dimensions: Precise definitions — focus as point of energy release underground vs. epicenter as surface projection
Depth classification: shallow (<70 km), intermediate (70–300 km), deep-focus (300–700 km) and their damage potential
Why shallow-focus earthquakes are most destructive despite lower magnitude
UPSC trap: Deep-focus earthquakes occur only in subduction zones (Benioff zone) — not at mid-ocean ridges or continental collision zones

concepts.name: Seismic Waves: P-waves (Primary) — Nature and Behaviour
key_dimensions: Compressional/longitudinal wave — particle motion parallel to wave propagation
Travel through all media (solid, liquid, gas) — fastest seismic wave; first to be recorded
P-wave shadow zone (103°–142°) — evidence for liquid outer core
UPSC trap: P-waves slow down (but do NOT stop) when passing through liquid — students often say they cannot travel through liquids at all

concepts.name: Seismic Waves: S-waves (Secondary) — Nature and Behaviour
key_dimensions: Shear/transverse wave — particle motion perpendicular to wave propagation
Cannot travel through liquids — key evidence for liquid outer core
S-wave shadow zone (>103°) — larger than P-wave shadow zone and why
UPSC trap: S-waves travel only through solids, so their complete absence beyond 103° is stronger evidence for liquid outer core than P-wave shadow zone

concepts.name: Surface Waves: Love and Rayleigh Waves — Characteristics and Damage
key_dimensions: Love waves — horizontal shear motion; travel faster than Rayleigh waves among surface waves
Rayleigh waves — elliptical retrograde motion; responsible for rolling ground motion felt during earthquakes
Surface waves have lowest frequency, longest wavelength, slowest speed — but cause maximum destruction
UPSC trap: Surface waves are derived from body waves at the surface — they are NOT independent; also Love waves have NO vertical component

concepts.name: Shadow Zones of Seismic Waves: Interpretation and Earth's Interior Evidence
key_dimensions: P-wave shadow zone between 103°–142° — explained by refraction at core-mantle boundary
S-wave shadow zone beyond 103° — explained by inability to pass through liquid outer core
How shadow zones together confirm the two-layer core model (liquid outer + solid inner)
UPSC trap: The inner core is solid — confirmed by P-waves being detected within the S-wave shadow zone at very high angles (PKiKP/PKIKP paths)

concepts.name: Richter Scale: Magnitude Measurement and Logarithmic Nature
key_dimensions: Measures amplitude of seismic waves recorded on seismograph — open-ended logarithmic scale
Each whole number = 10× increase in wave amplitude; ~31.6× increase in energy released
Limitations: saturates at ~8.0 (cannot distinguish very large earthquakes accurately)
UPSC trap: Richter scale measures magnitude (energy at source), NOT intensity (effect at a location) — students confuse with Mercalli scale

concepts.name: Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw): Modern Standard and Comparison with Richter
key_dimensions: Based on seismic moment — product of rigidity, fault area, and average slip; does not saturate
Why Mw replaced Richter for large earthquakes (e.g., 2004 Indian Ocean quake reported as Mw 9.1–9.3)
Continuity with Richter scale for moderate earthquakes — similar values below M~7
UPSC trap: Most modern magnitude reports use Mw, NOT Richter — UPSC questions may use 'Richter' colloquially for any magnitude scale

concepts.name: Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale: Measuring Earthquake Effects
key_dimensions: Roman numeral scale (I–XII) measuring perceived shaking and damage at a specific location
Intensity varies with distance from epicenter, local geology, building quality — same earthquake has multiple intensity values
Comparison with magnitude: magnitude is single value per earthquake; intensity varies spatially
UPSC trap: Higher intensity does NOT always mean higher magnitude — a moderate shallow earthquake near a settlement can have higher intensity than a deep high-magnitude event

concepts.name: Seismograph and Seismogram: Instrumentation and Reading
key_dimensions: Principle of inertia — suspended mass remains stationary while ground moves; relative motion recorded
Seismogram components — P-wave arrival, S-wave arrival, surface wave arrival used to calculate epicenter distance
Time-distance graph (travel-time curves) — P–S interval used to determine distance to epicenter
UPSC trap: A single seismograph gives distance but NOT direction; minimum three stations needed for epicenter triangulation

concepts.name: Global Seismic Belts: Circum-Pacific, Alpide, and Mid-Atlantic Ridge Zones
key_dimensions: Circum-Pacific Belt ('Ring of Fire') — ~80% of world's earthquakes; associated with subduction and volcanic activity
Alpide Belt (Mediterranean–Himalayan) — ~15% of earthquakes; continent-continent collision; less volcanic
Mid-Atlantic Ridge Belt — shallow-focus, moderate earthquakes; transform faults between ridge segments
UPSC trap: Alpide Belt passes through India (Himalayas, Andaman arc) — Himalayan earthquakes are shallow-focus collision type, NOT subduction type

concepts.name: India's Seismic Zonation: Zone II to Zone V Classification
key_dimensions: BIS seismic zone map — Zone II (least hazard) to Zone V (most hazard/highest MSK intensity VIII+)
Zone V areas: entire NE India, J&K, Himachal, Uttarakhand, parts of Gujarat (Kutch), Andaman & Nicobar
Intraplate seismicity of Peninsular India — Deccan Plateau considered stable but Koyna/Latur challenge this
UPSC trap: Delhi falls in Zone IV (high damage risk), NOT Zone V — a common misconception; also Zone I has been dropped from the current BIS map

concepts.name: Tsunami Generation: Seismic Trigger Conditions and Wave Characteristics
key_dimensions: Required conditions: submarine earthquake, magnitude >7, shallow focus (<50 km), vertical fault displacement (thrust/reverse fault)
Wave characteristics in open ocean — long wavelength (100s km), low height (<1 m), high speed (~800 km/h); transformation near shore
Shoaling effect — wavelength decreases, height increases dramatically near coast
UPSC trap: Strike-slip faults (horizontal motion) generally do NOT generate tsunamis — only dip-slip (vertical) faults do; 2004 quake was a megathrust (dip-slip) event

concepts.name: Liquefaction: Soil Behaviour During Earthquakes
key_dimensions: Mechanism — saturated, loosely packed sandy/silty soil loses shear strength when seismic waves increase pore water pressure
Conditions favouring liquefaction: high water table, young unconsolidated deposits, sandy/silty texture
Consequences: buildings sink/tilt, ground fissures, loss of bearing capacity — seen in Bhuj 2001
UPSC trap: Liquefaction is NOT melting of rock — it is a physical soil mechanics phenomenon; hard rock areas are immune but river floodplains and coastal areas are highly vulnerable

concepts.name: Aftershocks, Foreshocks, and Earthquake Swarms: Patterns and Significance
key_dimensions: Foreshocks — smaller events before mainshock; not reliably identifiable in advance (prediction challenge)
Aftershocks — stress redistribution after mainshock; follow Omori's Law (frequency decays over time); can be nearly as large as mainshock
Earthquake swarms — series of similar-magnitude events with no clear mainshock; common in volcanic and geothermal areas
UPSC trap: The largest aftershock is typically ~1.2 magnitude units smaller than mainshock (Bath's Law) — but exceptions exist; 2011 Tohoku had M7.7 aftershock after M9.0 mainshock

concepts.name: Earthquake Prediction vs. Early Warning Systems: Distinction and Limitations
key_dimensions: Long-term prediction (probabilistic) vs. short-term prediction (deterministic) — science cannot reliably predict exact time/location
Earthquake Early Warning (EEW) systems — detect P-waves and send alerts before slower, destructive S-waves and surface waves arrive (seconds to tens of seconds)
Seismic gap theory — identifying segments of active faults with no recent rupture as high-risk zones
UPSC trap: EEW is NOT earthquake prediction — it provides seconds of warning AFTER an earthquake has already started; Japan's J-Alert system is a real-world example

concepts.name: Seismic Hazard vs. Seismic Risk: Conceptual Distinction for Disaster Management
key_dimensions: Hazard — physical phenomenon (probability of ground shaking of given intensity at a location)
Risk — function of hazard × exposure × vulnerability; high hazard with low exposure = low risk
Why Himalayan cities (high hazard + high exposure + poor construction = extreme risk) vs. remote areas
UPSC trap: A region can have HIGH seismic hazard but LOW risk (sparse population, good construction) — UPSC disaster management questions often test this distinction in context of urban planning

concepts.name: Notable Indian Earthquakes: Bhuj, Uttarkashi, Latur — Geomorphic and Policy Lessons
key_dimensions: Bhuj 2001 (Mw 7.7) — intraplate, Zone V, liquefaction, lateral spreading; exposed poor enforcement of building codes
Latur 1993 — Deccan Plateau (supposedly stable), Zone III; challenged peninsular stability assumptions; led to BIS zone revision
Uttarkashi 1991 and Chamoli 1999 — Himalayan collision zone, shallow focus; landslide-triggered secondary hazards
UPSC trap: Latur earthquake led to re-evaluation of seismic zonation for Peninsular India and creation of NDMA framework — a policy-science linkage frequently tested
